description: For 7,000 years, the Egyptian Farmers pioneered agriculture along the Nile. Today, Fallahin Space Agency brings that legacy into the satellite era! We are a 6-member Cairo squad of Computer Engineering & CS students/grads specializing in ml, full-stack dev, data science, and 3D motion graphics—turning NASA Earth data into interactive projects (Our 6-member roster is pre-formed and full!)
summary:
MISSION EL GHEET ("el gheet" is Egyptian Arabic for "the field") is a working web app for the Field Shift challenge. A farmer near Sakha, in Egypt's Nile Delta, plans four seasons on one field by voice or by tapping pictures, in Egyptian Arabic or English.

The farmer starts with what can't change. Say, the last berseem (clover) cut on 20 May, because the cattle need it. Our Promise Test, a fixed set of rules, checks all four seasons against that promise and explains every clash in plain words. If the farmer lets something move, the app looks for options inside those limits and shows at most two.

For each candidate sowing date it compares the same 14 days in every year from 2001 to 2025, using NASA POWER daily weather at that spot. In our example, 28 May and 1 June differ by about 0.3 °C. That's less than the normal swing between years, and the app says so.

A plan is "feasible" only when approved local evidence backs every rule. No local agronomist has signed off our 27 crop rules yet, so the example plan is rejected and both new dates need review. The app doesn't guess.
details:
What it does

MISSION EL GHEET ("el gheet" is Egyptian Arabic for "the field") is a working prototype web app for one field near Sakha, Kafr El-Sheikh, in the Nile Delta. A farmer plans the next four growing seasons by voice or by tapping pictures, in Egyptian Arabic (right to left) or English. The farmer also says what must not change, for example the last berseem (clover) cut on 20 May, because the cattle need it.

The app then runs the Promise Test, a fixed set of rules that checks whether the plan breaks that promise or another hard rule, and says why in plain words. If the farmer allows some things to move, the app searches only inside those permissions, offers at most two alternatives, and shows what the weather was like near each candidate sowing date over 25 past years of NASA POWER data.

Every plan gets one of three results. "rejected" means a rule is clearly broken. "needs_review" means evidence is missing. "feasible" means every required rule is backed by approved evidence. The app never guesses its way to "feasible".

A main use: a protected fodder cut

This is the example we built and tested end to end, with a fictional farmer we call Uncle Hussein (scenario UH-001). His plan: berseem for fodder in winter 2026/27 with the last cut protected on 20 May 2027, then grain maize sown 15 May 2027, then wheat on 20 November, then grain sorghum on 1 June 2028. He lets the maize date move to 28 May or 1 June.

What the running app returns:

- The original plan is rejected (sowing_before_protected_cut). The maize would go in while the field is still kept for the berseem cut.

- Maize on 28 May: needs_review. Maize on 1 June: needs_review. No rule is broken, but the new maize harvest and field-release dates are unknown, and no local crop rule has been approved yet. The app does not make those dates up.

- Feasible alternatives: zero. The protected 20 May cut stays in every option.

Zero is the right answer today. There is no approved local evidence that would prove a full repair, so the app says "no sure alternative", keeps the original plan, and lists what an extension worker would need to check next. Under each result, a "What research says" section shows sourced notes from the reviewed knowledge base for each crop, and marks whether the farmer's date falls before, inside or after the sourced window. These notes are for reading. They never change a plan's status.

How it works

The planner core is a Python package, meg_core, written with the standard library only. Same input, same output. It holds the Promise Test, a bounded search for alternatives (up to 256 combinations by default, and it reports when the search was cut short), and a 12-crop catalogue graded by evidence level.

The agricultural knowledge base has 27 sourced rules for wheat, berseem, grain maize and grain sorghum (release sakha-agricultural-review-2026-11-14.1). Each rule records its source, location, scientific status and approval state. A rule can enforce a result only after local agronomic sign-off. Today 0 of 27 are signed off, which is why results come out rejected or needs_review and never feasible. Where two sources disagree, for example on the wheat sowing window, both are kept and the rule stays blocked.

The app offers the four crops that have reviewed-knowledge-base evidence. The other crops in the catalogue (rice, faba bean, sugar beet, Egyptian cotton, plus watermelon, strawberry, cantaloupe and harankash for information only) are shown greyed out and can't be picked yet.

The backend is a FastAPI REST API with SQLite storage. It turns the farmer's answers into a planner input, runs the Promise Test, saves an evidence card as a review draft, and renders every message from bilingual templates, each with a written form and a spoken form (numbers spelled out in Egyptian Arabic words). The frontend is a React app built for phone screens: picture tiles, push-to-talk speech input through the browser, and a spoken read-back of every fact before checking, including the unknown ones ("Berseem sowing date: unknown").

Data, and how it supports the use

We use NASA POWER daily data (Daily API v2.10.3, community AG) at 31.10°N, 30.95°E near Sakha, for 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2025: daily maximum and minimum temperature, dew point, humidity, wind, solar radiation, surface pressure and corrected precipitation. The raw files are stored with SHA-256 checksums, fill values (-999) are rejected, and all 9,131 daily rows were checked for gaps and duplicates. The app verifies checksums before use and never downloads data at run time.

From that record we compute FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0) and a seasonal climatology (2001-2018, 10th/50th/90th percentile per calendar day).

Season Replay uses this for the main example. For each candidate sowing date it takes the same 14-day window in every year from 2001 to 2025 and compares them. For the 28 May and 1 June windows, mean daily maximum temperature was 36.59 °C and 36.90 °C. The 0.30 °C gap is smaller than the year-to-year spread (standard deviation 1.33 and 1.51 °C), and the later window was hotter in 14 of 25 years, close to a coin toss. 14-day ET0 was 119.0 mm against 119.6 mm. So the weather gives no strong reason to prefer either date, and the screen says that. It also says "Historical 14-day planting-window comparison, not a full crop-season analysis".

ET0 is how much water the air would pull from a standard grass surface. It is not the crop's water use and not an irrigation amount, and the app labels it "Not irrigation". Weather results never change a plan's status.

We also tested machine-learning forecasts. A simple seasonal climatology beat both a Ridge regression (2019-2021 validation, daily max temperature MAE 2.53 °C for climatology against 2.58 °C for Ridge) and the Chronos-2 foundation model with LoRA fine-tuning (July-October 2026 holdout, 1.66 °C against 1.99 °C). So the app uses climatology for "typical conditions". Forecasting is an experimental side channel, and no forecast can decide whether a plan is feasible.

What works today, and how we checked it

Working in the delivered code: four-season plan entry in Arabic and English, by voice or taps; the Promise Test with protected commitments and reasons; bounded alternatives within the farmer's permissions; "What research says" notes; Season Replay with climatology; the bilingual evidence card saved as a review draft. The app also runs without a backend, using a labelled development adapter that replays real planner output for the UH-001 example only.

Checks we ran on 14 November 2026: planner 118 tests OK (3 skipped); backend 81 passed, 1 skipped; frontend typecheck, 30 unit tests and production build pass. The Season Replay numbers for UH-001 match an independent recomputation from the NASA POWER file to within 1e-14. The full UH-001 journey was clicked through in a browser against the running backend at 12 screen widths (360-1440 px), in both languages.

For a public demo the backend has per-client rate limits, request-size caps and a daily ceiling on voice calls. The app is public at https://mission-el-gheet.vercel.app/ (frontend on Vercel, backend on Render). It also runs on any laptop, CPU only, with no internet needed at run time; the commands are in AGENTS.md.

Next

Field tests with farmers near Sakha. Formal review and sign-off of the 27 rules by Sakha experts. Asking for harvest and field-release dates in the app. Adding more crops only once they have approved local calendars. Native Arabic review, real recorded voice and real crop pictures. Adding NASA GPM rainfall and MODIS field history. Later, other areas of the Delta.

Tools, languages, hardware

Python 3.12 (planner, climate code, backend). FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn and SQLite for the API. TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8 and Tailwind CSS 4 for the frontend, with the browser Web Speech API for speech input. Optional services: Google Gemini API (reading a spoken answer; its output is checked by fixed rules and confirmed by the farmer) and ElevenLabs (75 Arabic voice clips, generated offline). Data science: Python scripts for the NASA POWER download, FAO-56 ET0 and climatology, plus Ridge and Chronos-2 experiments for research only. Testing: pytest, unittest, Vitest, Playwright for screenshots. Dependencies are exact-pinned with hashed lock files and a 14-day minimum package age. Git and GitHub. Ordinary Windows and Linux laptops, CPU only.
